title: The Price of a Place in Line
intuition: A regulator must decide whose infrastructure project goes first but cannot verify how valuable or reliable a developer's project is. Collateral is then the only tool that makes developers report truthfully. The note computes the exact deposit needed for efficient priority, shows that it exceeds what either pivotal developer gains from priority, and shows that a priority lottery is optimal when collateral is scarcer.
statement: Efficient truthful implementation with individual rationality is possible if and only if the escrow limit satisfies $L \ge K$, where $K = \frac{c[s(1-r)a - r(1-s)b]}{s-r}$; moreover $K > csa$, so the required collateral exceeds both pivotal types' expected gains from priority.
summary: A developer whose project value $v \in \{a,b\}$ and completion probability $p \in \{r,s\}$ are private competes for priority against a fallback developer with a publicly known type; the second project is attempted only if the first fails, and project values are unverifiable. The regulator can use only an escrow of at most $L$, refunded according to reports, the priority lottery and observed completion outcomes. Efficiency gives priority exactly to high-value reports, although the pivotal high-value type $h=(b,r)$ values priority less than the low-value type $\ell=(a,s)$. When $L < K$, every DSIC mechanism has expected welfare loss at least $\min\{\mu_h\Delta_h, \mu_\ell(-\Delta_\ell)\}(1-L/K)_+$, and a priority lottery attains this bound for a family of two-point priors. The implementing deposit refunds more after failure than after success.
sources: Burguet, R., J.-J. Ganuza, and E. Hauk. 2012. "Limited liability and mechanism design in procurement." Games and Economic Behavior 76(1): 15-25. doi:10.1016/j.geb.2012.04.004.
Che, X., T. Li, J. Lu, and X. Zheng. 2022. "Deposit Requirements in Auctions." American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 14(4): 465-493. doi:10.1257/mic.20200206.

title: The Information Complexity of Nash Equilibrium
intuition: How many noisy observations of payoffs are needed to find an approximate Nash equilibrium of a small zero-sum game with high confidence? The answer depends only on the equilibrium mixing probabilities, is largest when equilibrium play is uniform, and can be far smaller than estimating every payoff first and then solving the game.
statement: For a $3 \times 3$ zero-sum game $A$ with a unique, completely mixed equilibrium $(p,q)$, learned from noisy $N(A_{ij},1)$ queries, the expected number of observations needed to return an $\varepsilon$-equilibrium with probability $1-\delta$ satisfies $\lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \varepsilon^2 \lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} \frac{M_{\varepsilon,\delta}(A)}{\log(1/\delta)} = C(p,q) := 2\left[\min_{w \in \Delta_9^\circ} F_{p,q}(w)\right]^2$, with $0 < C(p,q) \le 8$ and $C(p,q) = 8$ if and only if $p = q = (1/3,1/3,1/3)$.
summary: Each query of payoff entry $(i,j)$ returns an independent $N(A_{ij},1)$ observation, and a procedure must return strategies with duality gap at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ for every game in the class. The leading observation complexity, as confidence and then accuracy increase, is the constant $C(p,q)$, which depends on the game only through its equilibrium probabilities; $F_{p,q}(w)$ is a transport-type functional over couplings of $p$ and $q$ given a sampling allocation $w$ over the nine entries. The constant is maximal, equal to 8, exactly at uniform equilibrium, and for the family $A_r$ with equilibrium $(1-2r, r, r)$ it is of order $r^2$. By comparison, estimating all nine payoffs to maximum-norm error $\varepsilon$ has coefficient 18, and estimating payoffs to error $\varepsilon/2$ and then solving the game has coefficient 72. The proof applies the infinite-answer pure-exploration characterization of Poiani, Bernasconi and Celli (2026) and evaluates its small-accuracy limit through transportation duality.
sources: Poiani, R., Bernasconi, M., and Celli, A. 2026. "Pure Exploration with Infinite Answers." Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, PMLR 300, 2989-2997.
Kaplansky, I. 1945. "A Contribution to Von Neumann's Theory of Games." Annals of Mathematics 46(3): 474-479.

title: The Pre-FOMC Drift Lost Its Morning
intuition: Stocks have earned a well-known excess return in the hours before Federal Reserve announcements. Studies using daily closing prices conclude that this drift has faded, but it has moved rather than disappeared: since 2011 it is earned overnight before the announcement day, not during the morning of that day.
statement: The pre-FOMC announcement drift in SPY has not disappeared; its timing has changed. From September 2003 to March 2011 most of it accrued between the open and 2pm on the announcement day (29.1 bp, $t = 4.3$); after March 2011 that morning component is zero (1.5 bp), and the overnight return into the announcement day (17.2 bp, $t = 3.7$) is now essentially the whole drift.
summary: Lucca and Moench (2015) documented a large excess stock return in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements, and studies using daily closing prices report that it weakened after 2015. Using SPY from September 2003 to December 2024 (170 scheduled announcements), with CRSP open and close prices and TAQ quote mid-points at 2pm, the note splits the window from 2pm on the previous day to the close of the following day into seven legs and compares each leg on announcement days with all other days. The 2pm-to-2pm drift falls from 58.0 bp to 16.9 bp, and the fall of 27.6 bp in the morning leg has $t = -3.6$, while the overnight leg is stable at about 13 to 17 bp and holds separately in 2011-2015 and 2016-2024. Closing-price studies understate the remaining drift because returns after the announcement have been weak since 2011. The overnight result survives alternative price sources, the exclusion of 2020, winsorization, placebo nights and the removal of the 2011-2012 meetings with a 12:30pm statement.
sources: Boguth, O., Gregoire, V., and Martineau, C. 2019. "Shaping Expectations and Coordinating Attention: The Unintended Consequences of FOMC Press Conferences." Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 54(6): 2327-2353.
Kurov, A., Wolfe, M. H., and Gilbert, T. 2021. "The Disappearing Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift." Finance Research Letters 40.
Lucca, D. O., and Moench, E. 2015. "The Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift." Journal of Finance 70(1): 329-371.
Pan, J., and Peng, Q. 2024. "The Pre-FOMC Drift in Long-Term Treasury Bonds." Working paper, SSRN 4764451.
Data: CRSP daily stock file and TAQ quotes via WRDS; FOMC dates from the Federal Reserve Board.

title: Zipf's Law for US Cities, 2000-2024
intuition: Zipf's law, under which a city's size is inversely proportional to its rank, is often treated as a constant of urban economics. In US data for 2000-2024 it holds only for metropolitan areas at particular cut-offs; incorporated cities follow a clean power law, but with an exponent clearly above 1.
statement: In US data for 2000-2024, Zipf's law with $\zeta = 1$ fails for both common city definitions: for metropolitan areas the exponent for the largest 135 is about 1.1 and not statistically different from 1, but the rank-size relation is curved, so a single power law is rejected; for incorporated cities the relation is straight, but $\zeta \approx 1.45$ is statistically above 1.
summary: Zipf's law says that the number of cities larger than $S$ is proportional to $S^{-\zeta}$ with $\zeta = 1$, the value implied by city growth unrelated to size (Gabaix 1999). Using Census Bureau population files for metropolitan statistical areas (2010, 2020, 2024) and incorporated places (2000, 2010, 2020, 2024), the note estimates $\zeta$ by the rank minus one half regression of Gabaix and Ibragimov (2011) and applies their curvature test. For metropolitan areas the curvature statistic is $-2.3$ to $-2.7$ for the largest 135 and $-3.0$ for the largest 250, and the estimate falls from 1.42 for the top 50 to 0.90 for all metros, so $\zeta$ is within 0.05 of 1 only for cut-offs between about 190 and 320. For cities proper the curvature statistic is near zero, while $\zeta$ is 1.41 to 1.46 for the largest 135 ($t$ of 2.4 to 2.6 against 1). Both patterns are stable from 2000 to 2024, so an exponent of 1 appears only for metropolitan areas at particular cut-offs.
sources: Bee, M., Riccaboni, M., and Schiavo, S. 2013. "The Size Distribution of US Cities: Not Pareto, Even in the Tail." Economics Letters 120(2): 232-237.
Eeckhout, J. 2004. "Gibrat's Law for (All) Cities." American Economic Review 94(5): 1429-1451.
Gabaix, X. 1999. "Zipf's Law for Cities: An Explanation." Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3): 739-767.
Gabaix, X., and Ibragimov, R. 2011. "Rank - 1/2: A Simple Way to Improve the OLS Estimation of Tail Exponents." Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 29(1): 24-39.
Rozenfeld, H. D., Rybski, D., Gabaix, X., and Makse, H. A. 2011. "The Area and Population of Cities: New Insights from a Different Perspective on Cities." American Economic Review 101(5): 2205-2225.
Soo, K. T. 2005. "Zipf's Law for Cities: A Cross-Country Investigation." Regional Science and Urban Economics 35(3): 239-263.
Data: US Census Bureau population estimates files (public).

title: Who Bargains Next? Recognition and Cooperative Allocations
intuition: Who proposes after an offer is rejected looks like a procedural detail, but it changes the outcome of coalitional bargaining. If the player who rejects proposes next, patient players no longer reach the Shapley value: every player's deviation from an equal share is amplified.
statement: In three-player coalitional bargaining with proposer departure probability $q$, both protocols have a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium payoff vector with immediate efficient agreement: $E_0 = e + d(s-e)$ when the next proposer after a surviving rejection is drawn uniformly, and $E_1 = e + d(1+a)(s-e)$ when the rejector proposes next, where $s$ is the Shapley value, $e$ the equal split, $a = \delta(1-q)$ and $d = \delta q/(1-a)$. The patient limits are $s$ and $s + (1-q)(s-e)$, which coincide if and only if $c_1 = c_2 = c_3$.
summary: Hart and Mas-Colell (1996) showed that random proposers with a risk that a rejected proposer drops out lead patient players to the Shapley value. This note compares two anonymous protocols for three players with transferable utility that share coalition opportunities, discounting and departure risk, and differ only in who proposes after a surviving rejection: a uniformly drawn player ($P_0$) or the rejector ($P_1$). Every subgame-perfect equilibrium, including mixed and history-dependent ones, agrees immediately on the grand coalition, and each protocol has a unique payoff vector. Under $P_1$ every player's patient deviation from the equal share is multiplied by $2-q$, so players whose Shapley value exceeds one third gain and the others lose; for $q = 7/8$ and $(c_1, c_2, c_3) = (1/4, 1/20, 1/20)$ the patient payoffs are $(4/15, 11/30, 11/30)$ under $P_0$ and $(31/120, 89/240, 89/240)$ under $P_1$. Specifying who controls bargaining after disagreement is therefore part of specifying the outcome.
sources: Britz, V., Herings, P. J.-J., and Predtetchinski, A. 2014. "On the convergence to the Nash bargaining solution for action-dependent bargaining protocols." Games and Economic Behavior 86: 178-183.
Calvo, E., and Gutierrez-Lopez, E. 2016. "A strategic approach for the discounted Shapley values." Theory and Decision 80: 271-293.
Gul, F. 1989. "Bargaining Foundations of Shapley Value." Econometrica 57: 81-95.
Hart, S., and Mas-Colell, A. 1996. "Bargaining and Value." Econometrica 64: 357-380.
Kawamori, T. 2008. "A note on selection of proposers in coalitional bargaining." International Journal of Game Theory 37: 525-532.
Kawamori, T. 2016. "Hart-Mas-Colell implementation of the discounted Shapley value." Theory and Decision 81: 357-369.

title: The Pythagorean Expectation, 45 Seasons Later
intuition: Bill James's formula linking a baseball team's wins to its runs scored and allowed has worked unchanged in the 45 seasons since it was published. Records that beat the formula are mostly luck and do not carry over, so a team's quality is better read from its runs than from its wins.
statement: Bill James's Pythagorean expectation $W/L = (RS/RA)^k$ survives a 45-season out-of-sample test: the exponent is $k = 1.847$ on 1901-1980 and $k = 1.848$ on 1981-2025, the 1901-1980 fit predicts later wins with an error of about 4 per 162 games and explains 88% of their variation, and wins above or below the formula do not persist: about 92% disappears the next season.
summary: The Pythagorean expectation, published around 1980, relates a baseball team's ratio of wins to losses to its ratio of runs scored to runs allowed, and every season after 1980 provides a clean holdout sample. Using 2,706 Major League team-seasons from the Lahman Baseball Database, the note estimates $k$ as the slope of $\log(W/L)$ on $\log(RS/RA)$ before and after publication and finds the same value to the third decimal, with out-of-sample root mean squared error of 4.06 wins against 4.16 for James's original $k = 2$. The exponent varies by decade between 1.74 and 1.98 but has no trend, and letting it rise with runs per game does not improve the out-of-sample error. Wins above the formula (luck, with a standard deviation of 4.2 wins) have a next-season correlation of only 0.04 before 1980 and 0.08 after, and in forecasting next season's record the predicted share receives about three times the weight of the actual share. The same task, separating a persistent component from a large transitory one, arises when judging fund managers, executives or forecasters from short records.
sources: Davenport, C., and Woolner, K. 1999. "Revisiting the Pythagorean Theorem: Putting Bill James' Pythagorean Theorem to the Test." Baseball Prospectus.
Friendly, M., Dalzell, C., Monkman, M., and Murphy, D. 2026. "Lahman: Sean 'Lahman' Baseball Database." R package version 14.0-0.
James, B. 1980. The Bill James Baseball Abstract. Self-published.
Miller, S. J. 2007. "A Derivation of the Pythagorean Won-Loss Formula in Baseball." Chance 20(1): 40-48.
Data: Lahman Baseball Database (public).

title: Engel's Law Holds for Groceries, Not for Restaurants
intuition: Poorer households spend a larger share of their budget on food, and this still holds in US data up to 2024. The pattern comes entirely from groceries: spending on restaurants rises in proportion to the budget in every income group.
statement: In the US Consumer Expenditure Survey, Engel's law holds in every year from 1984 to 2024: across the five income groups the elasticity of food spending with respect to total spending averages 0.77 and is below one in all 41 years. The law is driven entirely by groceries (elasticity 0.58), while spending on food away from home has an elasticity of 1.07, above one in 40 of 41 years.
summary: Engel (1857) observed that poorer families spend a larger share of their budget on food, so that food has an income elasticity below one. Using published BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey means for each income fifth, 1984-2024, the note estimates each year's elasticity as the slope of log spending on log total expenditures across the five groups, separately for all food, groceries and eating out. In 2024 groceries fell from 11.0% of spending in the lowest fifth to 6.2% in the highest, while eating out took between 4.7% and 5.2% in every group; for the average household the food share fell from 14.7% in 1984-1993 to 12.8% in 2005-2019 and has not fallen since. The official US poverty line still rests on Orshansky's multiplier of three times a minimal food budget, whereas 2024 food shares of 15.7% in the lowest fifth and 12.9% on average would imply a multiplier of about 6 to 8. Because eating out rises at least in proportion to the budget, methods that use Engel curves to estimate CPI bias should rely on groceries rather than on all food.
sources: Chai, A., and Moneta, A. 2010. "Retrospectives: Engel Curves." Journal of Economic Perspectives 24(1): 225-240.
Costa, D. L. 2001. "Estimating Real Income in the United States from 1888 to 1994: Correcting CPI Bias Using Engel Curves." Journal of Political Economy 109(6): 1288-1310.
Engel, E. 1857. "Die Productions- und Consumtionsverhaeltnisse des Koenigreichs Sachsen." Zeitschrift des Statistischen Bureaus des Koeniglich Saechsischen Ministeriums des Innern 8-9: 1-54.
Hamilton, B. W. 2001. "Using Engel's Law to Estimate CPI Bias." American Economic Review 91(3): 619-630.
Houthakker, H. S. 1957. "An International Comparison of Household Expenditure Patterns, Commemorating the Centenary of Engel's Law." Econometrica 25(4): 532-551.
Orshansky, M. 1965. "Counting the Poor: Another Look at the Poverty Profile." Social Security Bulletin 28(1): 3-29.
Data: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditure Survey (public).

title: Wisdom of Crowds with Many Separate Groups: A Correction to Golub and Jackson (2010)
intuition: Golub and Jackson (2010) showed that a society that averages its neighbors' opinions learns the truth exactly when no one keeps a large influence. That equivalence breaks when the society splits into many separate groups: each group may learn well, yet with so many groups at least one of them is almost sure to end far from the truth. The note gives a counterexample, a corrected statement, and a sharp rule for equal-sized groups: their size must grow faster than the logarithm of their number.
statement: For networks with a growing number of separate closed groups, vanishing maximal influence $s_1(n) \to 0$ does not imply wisdom: a society of $4^m$ groups of $m$ agents satisfies every assumption of Golub and Jackson (2010) with $s_1(n) = 1/m$, yet with probability $1-(1-2^{-m})^{4^m} \to 1$ some agent ends at belief one when the truth is one half. In general, the society is wise if and only if $\sum_{c=1}^{K_n} \Pr(|Y_c - \mu| > \varepsilon) \to 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, where $Y_c$ is the consensus of closed group $c$; the original equivalence holds when the number of groups $K_n$ is bounded, and for $K_n$ equally weighted groups of size $m_n$ with fair-coin signals, the society is wise if and only if $m_n \to \infty$ and $(\log K_n)/m_n \to 0$.
summary: Under naive DeGroot learning, Proposition 2 of Golub and Jackson (2010) states that a sequence of convergent networks is wise, meaning all agents are simultaneously close to the truth, if and only if the largest influence vanishes, and the paper states that its results apply to all convergent networks. The proof shows that each agent learns individually, but wisdom requires all agents to be right at the same time, and with many independent closed groups the two requirements differ: in a network of $4^m$ groups of $m$ agents with fair-coin signals, the largest influence is $1/m$ and Theorem 4's balance and minimal in-dispersion conditions hold, yet the probability that some group is unanimously wrong tends to one. The corrected proposition characterizes wisdom by the sum over groups of each group's probability of error, keeps the 'only if' direction, restores the original equivalence when the number of closed groups is bounded (including every strongly connected network), and gives a distribution-free sufficient condition, $\max_c Q_c (1 + \log K_n) \to 0$. For equally weighted groups this condition is sharp: using Hoeffding's inequality and a method-of-types bound, the society is wise exactly when group size grows faster than the logarithm of the number of groups. Vanishing maximal influence still makes the society accurate on average, Theorem 1 is not exposed because its out-dispersion condition bounds the number of closed groups, and the paper's central message, that a society learns well only if no agent's influence stays large, is unaffected.
sources: Cover, T. M., and Thomas, J. A. 2006. Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley.
Golub, B., and Jackson, M. O. 2010. "Naive Learning in Social Networks and the Wisdom of Crowds." American Economic Journal: Microeconomics 2(1): 112-149.
Hoeffding, W. 1963. "Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables." Journal of the American Statistical Association 58(301): 13-30.

title: Growth in Endogenous Production Networks Needs Compatible Recipes: A Correction to Acemoglu and Azar (2020)
intuition: Acemoglu and Azar (2020) show that when firms choose their suppliers, the growth rate equals the rate at which the best technologies improve, multiplied by the full input-output network. That product assumes firms can use the best technology and keep all their important suppliers at the same time. When the best new technologies require dropping an important supplier, firms must give up either productivity or network amplification, and growth falls short of the formula.
statement: Under the stated assumptions of Acemoglu and Azar (2020), the growth formula of their Theorem 6, $g = D \sum_{i,j} \beta_i L_{ij}$ with $L = (I-\alpha)^{-1}$, is false: in an economy that satisfies every assumption and where the formula predicts $g = 2$, equilibrium growth is $4/3$, and a second example gives $4$. The formula holds, and the condition is also necessary, under compatibility: for every industry $i$ and every finite set $H$ of suppliers with positive shares, the best recipe that keeps $H$ satisfies $M_i^H(t)/t \to D$, together with a uniform bound on frontier productivity across industries.
summary: In the endogenous production network model of Acemoglu and Azar (2020), industries choose supplier sets from all available input combinations, and Theorem 6 states that growth equals the frontier productivity rate $D$ times the Leontief multiplier of the full potential network. The note gives two economies that satisfy every stated assumption but contradict the formula. In the first, recipes that use the supplier carrying half of all input shares are unproductive, so every firm drops it and growth is $4/3$ rather than $2$; the same holds with independent continuous productivity draws, where growth can take any value in $[4/3, 2)$. In the second, late-arriving industries with very high productivity levels raise growth to $4$, because the assumption on the frontier holds industry by industry but not uniformly. The failures trace to two specific steps in the proof and overturn Corollaries 1 to 3, the upper bound of Theorem 7 and Theorem B3, while sustained positive growth, the benchmark with iid Gumbel or exponential draws and the static model survive; the corrected theorem holds exactly when frontier technologies are compatible with the existing supplier base.
sources: Acemoglu, D., and Azar, P. D. 2020. "Endogenous Production Networks." Econometrica 88(1): 33-82, and its online supplement.

title: Do US Firm Sizes Follow Zipf's Law? In the Middle, Yes. At the Top, No
intuition: Axtell (2001) found that US firm sizes follow Zipf's law: a firm ten times larger is ten times rarer, from the smallest firms to the largest. In public data up to 2023 this holds remarkably well between about 5 and 10,000 employees, but not at the top: Zipf predicts a largest US firm of about 12 million employees, while the largest actual employer has about 2 million worldwide. The giants are too few and too small, which matters because Zipf is the case in which shocks to the largest firms move the whole economy.
statement: In the Census Business Dynamics Statistics for 1978-2023, the share of US firms with at least $s$ employees falls like $s^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha$ between 0.94 and 1.00 for $5 \le s \le 10{,}000$ in every year, as Zipf's law requires. The law fails at the top: the mean size of firms with 10,000 or more employees implies a tail exponent of about 1.32 in 2023 (a Hill estimate of 1.29 on the 200 largest Compustat employers), and on employees, sales and market value alike the 50 largest listed firms have exponents between about 1.4 and 1.9.
summary: Zipf's law for firm sizes, $\Pr(S \ge s) \propto s^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha = 1$, is the benchmark outcome of random proportional growth and governs whether idiosyncratic shocks to large firms matter for aggregate fluctuations (Gabaix 2011). Using the public Census Business Dynamics Statistics for 1978-2023 and Compustat for the largest employers, the note finds slopes between 0.94 and 1.00 from 5 to 10,000 employees in every year, too few firms with 1-4 employees, and a clearly thinner top. Extrapolating Zipf from the 1,210 firms with 10,000 or more employees in 2023 predicts a largest firm of about 12 million employees, against 2.1 million for the largest actual employer, and matching the observed mean of that class requires an exponent of 1.32. By headcount the top has moved toward Zipf, from exponents of 1.7-1.9 in the 1980s and 1990s to about 1.35 today, while the middle of the distribution did not change. Measuring size by sales or market value does not rescue the law: the 500 largest listed firms look Zipf on every measure, but the 50 largest are too similar in size on all of them.
sources: Axtell, R. L. 2001. "Zipf Distribution of U.S. Firm Sizes." Science 293: 1818-1820.
Gabaix, X. 2011. "The Granular Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations." Econometrica 79(3): 733-772.
Kondo, I. O., Lewis, L. T., and Stella, A. 2023. "Heavy Tailed but not Zipf: Firm and Establishment Size in the United States." Journal of Applied Econometrics 38(5): 767-785.
U.S. Census Bureau. Business Dynamics Statistics, 1978-2023 release.
Data: Census Business Dynamics Statistics (public) and Compustat.

title: Does Stamp Duty Make UK Shares Cheap? Prices Say No, Takeovers Say Maybe
intuition: The UK charges a 0.5% tax every time a UK share is bought, and a common argument holds that this makes UK shares cheap and UK companies easy takeover targets. If buyers priced in every future payment of the tax, the discount would be about 3% for the median stock and larger for stocks that trade often. In the two settings where only the tax differs, prices show no such discount; the only support comes from takeover bids, and it may reflect UK takeover rules rather than the tax.
statement: If buyers capitalize all future stamp duty, a UK share's price discount is about $0.005\,T/r$, where $T$ is annual turnover and $r$ the discount rate. When the tax on AIM shares was abolished (announced 20 March 2013), the slope of AIM returns on turnover was $-0.0025$ (s.e. $0.0012$) against a predicted $+0.0625$, and the taxed London line of Unilever traded on average 0.2% above its untaxed Dutch twin in 2006-2020 against a predicted 3.4% below. Across 15 European markets, UK bid probability rises with turnover more steeply than in untaxed markets, but a within-UK test cannot rule out no effect.
summary: The UK's 0.5% stamp duty on share purchases is often blamed for cheap UK valuations, foreign investors' retreat and takeovers of UK companies; if buyers capitalize every future payment, the price discount is about $0.005\,T/r$, around 3% for the median UK stock with $r = 8\%$. When AIM shares became exempt in 2013-14, AIM stocks beat still-taxed small Main Market firms by only 0.49% on the announcement day, an unremarkable spread, and frequently traded stocks gained no more than rarely traded ones, although the tax predicts up to a 5.5% gain; AIM turnover rose by about 3.5%, but foreign institutional ownership did not change measurably. Companies with two share lines show no tax discount either: Unilever's London line traded at parity with its Dutch twin for 14 years, Carnival's London line traded at a premium for most of 2004-16, and RELX's London line traded 3.8% above its Dutch line in 2015-18. Across 109,000 firm-years in 15 European markets, UK companies whose shares trade more are more likely to receive a bid, more steeply than in untaxed markets, but this cross-country pattern may reflect UK takeover rules, and the within-UK test after the AIM exemption is too imprecise to confirm it. The estimates are presented as first-pass and differ from earlier evidence that UK prices rose when stamp duty was cut from 2% in the 1980s.
sources: Amihud, Y., and Mendelson, H. 1986. "Asset Pricing and the Bid-Ask Spread." Journal of Financial Economics 17: 223-249.
Bond, S., Hawkins, M., and Klemm, A. 2004. "Stamp Duty on Shares and its Effect on Share Prices." IFS Working Paper 04/11.
Froot, K., and Dabora, E. 1999. "How Are Stock Prices Affected by the Location of Trade?" Journal of Financial Economics 53: 189-216.
Data: Datastream, FTSE AIM All-Share constituent lists, SDC Platinum and FactSet.

title: Five Small Errors in Bayesian Persuasion
intuition: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) founded information design, and a line-by-line check confirms its main theorems: with finitely many states, the sender's best signal is found by concavifying his payoff, an optimum exists, and it needs no more signal realizations than there are states. Five statements in the fine print are wrong as written, including a popular rule of thumb that two concave functions mean persuasion cannot help, and the web appendix's formula for infinitely many states. Each has a one-line fix.
statement: The main theorems of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) hold, but five statements do not: (1) with infinitely many states the value must be the closed convex hull, the smallest upper semicontinuous concave function above $\hat v$, since in an example meeting all the web appendix's assumptions its formula gives the sender 0 while full revelation gives 1; (2) a concave receiver action and a concave sender payoff do not rule out gains from persuasion, as with action $\sqrt{p}$ and sender payoff $-a$; (3) in the lobbying application with $\alpha < 1/2$, no disclosure is optimal but not uniquely; (4) a worked example ignores the constraint $a \ge 0$, so its bound is $(1 + E[\omega])/2$ rather than 1; (5) Proposition 2's genericity claim needs every action to be uniquely optimal at some belief.
summary: Bayesian persuasion characterizes the sender's optimal value as the concave closure of his payoff as a function of the receiver's belief; with finitely many states this is correct, an optimum exists and at most as many signal realizations as states are needed, and an exact-arithmetic check on 200 random finite games agrees. The web appendix's extension to compact state spaces uses the convex hull without closure, which contains only finite mixtures of beliefs: with a state uniform on $[0,1]$ and a receiver who guesses only when certain, every finite signal yields 0 for the sender while full revelation yields 1, and the fix is the closed convex hull, under which existence survives. The rule of thumb that persuasion cannot help when the receiver's action and the sender's payoff are both concave fails because composing concave functions preserves concavity only if the outer function is increasing: with action $\sqrt{p}$ and sender payoff $-a$, full disclosure beats silence at $p = 1/4$ ($-1/4$ against $-1/2$). In the lobbying application any signal that keeps every posterior mean at the prior mean is optimal for $\alpha < 1/2$, a worked example's bound becomes $1/2$ against a true optimum of $1/3$ once negative actions are ruled out, and Proposition 2 needs the stronger assumption that every action is uniquely optimal at some belief, which the web appendix already states. None of the errors affects the main theorems, but the rule of thumb is the kind of shortcut applied work reuses, and the appendix formula is cited as the reference result for continuous states.
sources: Dworczak, P., and Kolotilin, A. "The Persuasion Duality." Working paper.
Kamenica, E., and Gentzkow, M. 2011. "Bayesian Persuasion." American Economic Review 101(6): 2590-2615, and Web Appendix (October 2010).

title: Urban Growth Replicates, With Three Fixes
intuition: Duranton and Puga (2023) estimate that relaxing planning limits in seven expensive US cities would raise national output by about 8%. An independent rewrite of their public code reproduces every headline number exactly, and that figure survives. Three coding errors change smaller numbers: freezing cities at their 1950 sizes costs about a fifth of consumption rather than a quarter, and Los Angeles enters the policy by only 22 dollars.
statement: Re-coded from the authors' public files, the headline results of Duranton and Puga (2023) reproduce to six decimals, including the 7.95% output gain when seven cities expand. Three coding errors are confirmed: the consumption loss from freezing cities at their 1950 sizes is 19.4%, not 26.8%; the seven-city consumption gain is 2.11%, not 2.16%; and Los Angeles clears the policy's 200,000 dollar price cutoff by 22 dollars under a conversion that depends on the omitted city, although every standard conversion keeps it in. City edges spread with population at elasticity 0.41 rather than the model's 1, but urban costs measured directly rise at elasticity 0.104, close to the model's 0.11.
summary: Duranton and Puga (2023) model incumbents who use planning rules to cap city size and find that relaxing permits in seven expensive US cities would raise output by 7.95%. Porting the authors' Stata programs to Python reproduces their regressions and every headline number; only regressions on restricted NLSY79 and NHTS locations could not be re-run. Three errors are confirmed. Log prices are converted to dollars with the squared standard error of each city dummy, which depends on the omitted city: Los Angeles clears the cutoff by 22 dollars, misses it by 302 dollars (output gain 5.68%) with itself omitted or with no correction, and lies between 226,000 and 229,000 dollars under residual variance, Duan smearing or full prediction variance, which keep the same seven cities. The frozen-city calculation credits newcomers with incumbent consumption, contrary to the paper's own accounting, so the loss is 19.4% rather than 26.8%; the original figure holds only if permit payments are rebated, in which case the seven-city consumption gain would be 4.15%. Stata's min() ignoring missing values drops 774,360 residents of ten emptied cities, and counting them moves that gain from 2.16% to 2.11%. Equation (29)'s exact Pareto distribution of city sizes requires continuous time, although approximate Zipf survives. The linear city implies edge distance proportional to population, while the data give elasticity 0.41 (s.e. 0.02); center house prices plus marginal consumption rise at 0.104 (s.e. 0.010), close to the model's cost elasticity of 0.11, so the mechanism holds in reduced form.
sources: Duranton, G., and Puga, D. 2023. "Urban Growth and Its Aggregate Implications." Econometrica 91(6): 2219-2259, and replication files (diegopuga.org/data/urbangrowth).
Gabaix, X. 1999. "Zipf's Law for Cities: An Explanation." Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3): 739-767.
Data: authors' public replication files.

title: No-Arbitrage Does Not Imply an Equivalent Calibrated Pricing Measure
intuition: When a stock trades over two dates and options on its final price are priced by the market, one usually expects that ruling out arbitrage guarantees a pricing measure that agrees with the physical probabilities on which events are possible, prices every option correctly and makes the stock a fair game. In a simple, well-behaved market this fails: there is no arbitrage, yet every pricing measure that fits the option prices ignores a state that has physical probability one half.
statement: In a two-date semistatic market with bounded prices, a physical law $P$ that is itself a martingale, and option-implied terminal law $\nu$ with $1/2 \le dP_Y/d\nu < 3/2$, there is no arbitrage, yet no calibrated martingale measure is equivalent to $P$: the only calibrated martingale measure absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ gives zero probability to an intermediate state of physical probability $1/2$. In the family of such chain markets with weights $(t_n)$, no-arbitrage holds if and only if $\sum_n 2^n t_n = \infty$, while an equivalent calibrated martingale measure exists if and only if $\inf_k 2^{2k} t_{2k} > 0$.
summary: Nutz, Wiesel and Zhao (2023) assume a calibrated martingale measure equivalent to the physical law with finite relative entropy and leave its characterization in terms of trading strategies as an open problem. The note shows that ordinary no-arbitrage is not that characterization. The counterexample links infinitely many two-point martingale rows in a single chain with weights $t_n = 2^{-n}/(n \log 2)$, plus one extra row of physical probability one half. Calibrating to the terminal law propagates any weight on the extra row along the chain with alternating sign, so some even row would need negative probability; an arbitrage exploiting this would need an option payoff that doubles at each step down the chain, which is not integrable. The construction extends the non-closedness of semistatic outcomes found by Acciaio, Larsson and Schachermayer (2017) to a regular setting with a fixed physical law. With a closure condition the characterization returns through known results: by the Kreps-Yan theorem an equivalent calibrated measure exists if and only if the weak-star closure of the superhedging cone contains no free lunch, and a finite-entropy one exists if and only if no sequence of trades drives the expected exponential shortfall of a loss on any event down to its no-loss value.
sources: Acciaio, B., Larsson, M., and Schachermayer, W. 2017. "The Space of Outcomes of Semi-Static Trading Strategies Need Not Be Closed." Finance and Stochastics 21: 741-751.
Delbaen, F., Grandits, P., Rheinlaender, T., Samperi, D., Schweizer, M., and Stricker, C. 2002. "Exponential Hedging and Entropic Penalties." Mathematical Finance 12: 99-123.
Frittelli, M. 2000. "The Minimal Entropy Martingale Measure and the Valuation Problem in Incomplete Markets." Mathematical Finance 10: 39-52.
Kreps, D. M. 1981. "Arbitrage and Equilibrium in Economies with Infinitely Many Commodities." Journal of Mathematical Economics 8: 15-35.
Nutz, M., Wiesel, J., and Zhao, L. 2023. "Martingale Schroedinger Bridges and Optimal Semistatic Portfolios." Finance and Stochastics 27: 233-254.
Yan, J.-A. 1980. "Caracterisation d'une classe d'ensembles convexes de L1 ou H1." Seminaire de Probabilites XIV, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 784: 220-222.

title: Rough Heston Variance at Zero: Negative Moments, Conditional Paths and a Test for the Zero Event
intuition: In the rough Heston model the instantaneous variance is exactly zero with positive probability at every date. Without drift, the variance also puts so much probability just above zero that the expected inverse variance is infinite even after the zero atom is excluded. One root of a Gamma-function equation sets both how much probability lies near zero and how fast the expected variance falls into a zero.
statement: In the drift-free rough Heston model with Hurst parameter $H \in (0, 1/2)$, $E[V_t^{-q}; V_t > 0] < \infty$ if and only if $q < \delta_\beta$, where $\delta_\beta = (p_\beta - \beta)/(2H) \in (0,1)$ and $p_\beta$ solves a Gamma-function equation, so $E[V_t^{-1}; V_t > 0] = \infty$ for every $H$. Conditional on $V_T = 0$, the expected variance path is $v \sum_n A_n (1 - s/T)^{\rho_n}$ with positive weights summing to one and leading exponent $\rho_\beta = 2H(1 + \delta_\beta)$, and $\{V_T = 0\} = \{\int_0^T V_s (T-s)^{-2H-1} ds < \infty\}$ almost surely.
summary: The rough Heston variance reaches zero with positive probability at every fixed date, and without drift the atom is known in closed form. Using the affine transform formula and the maximal solution of the fractional Riccati equation, the note compares the gap between the maximal and unit Riccati solutions with powers of time through a first-contact property of the Riemann-Liouville derivative. This shows that negative moments on the event of positive variance are finite exactly below a cutoff $\delta_\beta$, which lies strictly between zero and one for every Hurst parameter (about 0.26 at $H = 0.25$, 0.59 at $H = 0.1$ and 0.08 at $H = 0.4$), and that $\log P(0 < V_t \le x)/\log x \to \delta_\beta$. Conditioning on zero variance at $T$ adds an explicit drift, and the conditional mean solves a renewal equation whose Laplace transform is $1/\Psi$ with $\Psi(z) = z + \lambda_\beta \Gamma(z+1)/\Gamma(z+\beta)$; it is a positive mixture of powers of the time remaining, led by $\rho_\beta = 2H(1 + \delta_\beta)$ with second exponent exactly $2\beta$. The zero event coincides with finiteness of one weighted integral of past variance, whose conditional mean is proportional to minus the log probability of the zero, an instance of the entropy-energy identity. Finally, two exact solutions driven by the same Brownian motion can separate only by changing sign from the first instant; pathwise uniqueness remains open.
sources: Abi Jaber, E., Larsson, M., and Pulido, S. 2019. "Affine Volterra Processes." Annals of Applied Probability 29: 3155-3200.
Bourdon, A., and Jeannin, T. 2026. "Moments in Rough Bergomi and Boundary Attainment in Rough Heston." arXiv:2606.07482.
Friesen, M., Gerhold, S., and Wiedermann, K. 2026. "Boundary Behaviour of the Volterra Square-Root Process." arXiv:2606.07290.
Kuznetsov, A., Kyprianou, A. E., and Pardo, J. C. 2012. "Meromorphic Levy Processes and Their Fluctuation Identities." Annals of Applied Probability 22: 1101-1135.
Lehec, J. 2013. "Representation Formula for the Entropy and Functional Inequalities." Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques 49: 885-899.
Mytnik, L., and Salisbury, T. S. 2015. "Uniqueness for Volterra-Type Stochastic Integral Equations." arXiv:1502.05513.

Promel, D. J., and Scheffels, D. 2025. "Pathwise Uniqueness for Singular Stochastic Volterra Equations with Hoelder Coefficients." Stochastics and Partial Differential Equations: Analysis and Computations.
Samko, S. G., Kilbas, A. A., and Marichev, O. I. 1993. Fractional Integrals and Derivatives: Theory and Applications. Gordon and Breach.

title: The Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle Is Back
intuition: Feldstein and Horioka (1980) found that countries that save more also invest more, almost one for one, as if capital could not cross borders. By the mid-2000s the link had nearly vanished. In World Bank data up to 2024 it has returned: across OECD countries, about half of a country's extra saving again shows up as extra investment at home, as in the 1980s, because current-account imbalances have shrunk.
statement: Across the 38 OECD countries, the slope of the period-average investment rate on the period-average national saving rate fell from 0.56 in 1980-89 and 0.65 in 1990-99 to 0.16 (s.e. 0.11) in 2000-07 and has returned to 0.51 (s.e. 0.06) in 2016-24; across all countries with population above one million it rose from 0.00 to 0.54 (s.e. 0.06).
summary: If capital moved freely, a country's investment would not depend on its own saving, yet Feldstein and Horioka (1980) found a cross-country slope of investment on saving close to 0.9 for 16 OECD countries in 1960-74. Using the World Development Indicators for 1980-2024, the note runs the same regression for successive periods, one observation per country, with robust standard errors. Because the current account equals saving minus investment, the slope equals $1 - \mathrm{cov}(CA,S)/\mathrm{var}(S)$ and falls when high savers run large surpluses. The OECD slope fell to 0.16 in 2000-07 and is 0.51 in 2016-24, with 2008-15 in between at 0.43; the rebound survives a balanced panel, dropping financial centers and oil exporters, using domestic instead of national saving, and counting only fixed investment, and in the euro area excluding Ireland and Luxembourg the slope moved from about zero to 0.41. The mechanism is in the current accounts: their cross-country standard deviation rose from 2.5% of GDP in the 1980s to 5.9% in 2000-07 and is now 3.9%, while the spread of saving rates changed little. The slope summarizes how far investment tracks saving and is not a clean measure of capital mobility, but it implies that about half of a gap in national saving now shows up as a gap in domestic investment.
sources: Blanchard, O., and Giavazzi, F. 2002. "Current Account Deficits in the Euro Area: The End of the Feldstein-Horioka Puzzle?" Brookings Papers on Economic Activity 2002(2): 147-209.
Feldstein, M., and Horioka, C. 1980. "Domestic Saving and International Capital Flows." Economic Journal 90(358): 314-329.
Obstfeld, M., and Rogoff, K. 2000. "The Six Major Puzzles in International Macroeconomics: Is There a Common Cause?" NBER Macroeconomics Annual 15: 339-390.
Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators (public).
